lead.headline: Ninth Circuit says California owed water rights holders a hearing before its 2021 drought cutoffs
lead.dek: A unanimous panel revived due process claims over curtailments on two Sacramento River tributaries, a ruling that could reshape how the state handles the next dry year.
body: A unanimous Ninth Circuit panel on November 24 reinstated due process claims brought by Stanford Vina Ranch Irrigation, Los Molinos Mutual Water and Peyton Pacific, which hold most of the water rights on Deer Creek and Mill Creek, two Sacramento River tributaries in Tehama County. They challenged the State Water Resources Control Board's 2021 emergency curtailment, which stopped diversions by 22 rights holders irrigating some 11,000 acres of orchards and pasture after Governor Gavin Newsom declared a drought emergency and agencies moved to protect salmon and steelhead.

A Sacramento trial judge had treated the emergency regulations and curtailment orders as legislative, which requires no individual hearing. Writing for the panel, Judge Lawrence VanDyke found them adjudicatory because they targeted a small, identifiable group of rights holders, so those holders were owed notice and a meaningful hearing before losing the right to divert. He wrote that the distinction "turns on the character of the action, rather than its label." The plaintiffs said they got a five minute public comment period and no chance to cross examine the state's witnesses.

In a separate memorandum the panel upheld the dismissal of the companies' takings claims, noting that compensation can be pursued through an inverse condemnation suit in California state court. The ruling does not change current water allocations, and the case now proceeds on the revived claims. The plaintiffs' attorney said the state has stopped their diversions four times in seven years; the Attorney General's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

pipe.source: Deer Creek and Mill Creek, Sacramento River tributaries in Tehama County, supply the diversions at issue.
pipe.treat: The case concerns rights, not treatment; the diverted creek water goes to farms largely as is.
pipe.use: The 2021 order hit 22 rights holders who irrigate some 11,000 acres of orchards, pasture and other uses.
pipe.reuse: The ruling does not address reuse; curtailment risk is one reason growers weigh storage and recycled supply.
pipe.discharge: Curtailment kept water in the creeks for salmon and steelhead during the 2021 drought.

use.text: Holders on small, named streams now have a stronger claim to a hearing first.
Fast drought orders aimed at a few diverters may need hearings built in.
Curtailment risk remains, but the process behind it is now contestable.
Expect more litigated, slower curtailments across Ninth Circuit states.

briefs.headline: Sciens Water buys Roberts Filter Group, a filtration maker founded in 1889, as its third platform
briefs.text: Sciens Water Opportunities Fund II closed its purchase of Roberts Filter Group, a Coatesville, Pennsylvania maker of gravity filters, underdrains and air scour systems, on November 9 and announced it on November 12. Family owned for more than a century, the company reports more than 4,500 filtration systems installed on six continents and more than 35 active patents, with long standing customers including Baltimore, Philadelphia and Puerto Rico's water authority. Matt Roberts stays on as chief executive. The announcement gave no price.
briefs.why: Engineered filtration for large utilities joins Sciens's regulated utility and decentralized treatment platforms, a bet on steady municipal plant spending.

briefs.headline: UN General Assembly makes the water conference a fixture, every three years from 2031
briefs.text: The General Assembly on November 23 adopted by consensus a resolution tabled by the UAE and Senegal that holds a UN Water Conference every three years starting in 2031, after the meetings already agreed for 2026 and 2028. The Secretary-General is asked to report at least six months before the 2031 conference, and the meetings are financed outside the regular UN budget. The next conference, co-hosted by the UAE and Senegal, runs December 8 to 10 in Abu Dhabi. Before 2023, the UN had held only one, in Mar del Plata in 1977.
briefs.why: A standing calendar gives governments, development banks and suppliers a regular deadline for water commitments and financing.

briefs.headline: Cheyenne's utility says data centers took about 2% of its water sales in 2025
briefs.text: The Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities sold about 3.5 billion gallons of water in 2025, and 93 million gallons went to data centers, Frank Strong, its engineering and water resource division manager, told Cowboy State Daily. He said actual use came in well below what operators first proposed, as newer chips can run at higher temperatures and need less water based cooling.
briefs.why: Metered utility data, not early projections, is starting to anchor the data center water debate. Drier basins will still want campus by campus numbers.

briefs.headline: UK says water supply no longer stalls any planned Greater Cambridge development
briefs.text: A progress report from the housing and environment ministries, published November 20, said the Environment Agency has withdrawn objections raised since 2022 to more than 9,000 homes and 500,000 square meters of commercial space, after Cambridge Water updated its water resources plan in March 2025. The package includes 2,048 social homes retrofitted for water efficiency, a Grafham to Cambridge transfer of up to 26 megaliters a day from 2032, and the proposed Fens Reservoir at up to 87 megaliters a day, which still needs a Development Consent Order.
briefs.why: Water has become a gating item for housing and lab space. Cambridge shows efficiency, metering and transfers unlocking approvals before new reservoirs arrive.

company.name: VA Tech Wabag
company.headline: Wabag's order book passed ₹20,000 crore, then Saudi Arabia pulled a big one
company.body: The Chennai based water treatment and desalination contractor reported first half revenue up 20% to about ₹1,887 crore and net profit up 29% to about ₹195 crore for the period to September 30, with net cash for a 15th straight quarter. Chairman and managing director Rajiv Mittal pointed to two large desalination orders, a seawater plant in Kuwait and a plant at Jamnagar in India. Management said revenue growth could reach the top of its 15% to 20% guidance. Nine days later the Saudi Water Authority cancelled the 300,000 cubic meter a day Yanbu award, and the company said it is seeking the reasons before deciding next steps.

leader.name: Yang Seung-jo
leader.role: Chief executive, Korea Water Resources Corporation (K-water)

figs.l: Daily supply planned for Honam fabs

leader.body: Yang has started his term at K-water's helm on the chip file. His first official field trip, on November 18, was to SK hynix's Yongin cluster to discuss timely supply and plans to localize ultrapure water production. On November 20 he inspected Juam and Dongbok dams, the main sources for the planned Honam semiconductor complex, where K-water plans to supply about 600,000 cubic meters a day and build 1.06 million of capacity to cover future demand and drought. Dongbok Dam is being raised 15 meters so it can send 300,000 cubic meters a day to the complex.

supplier.name: Kemira
supplier.headline: Kemira is buying its way into industrial water services while raw material costs squeeze margins
body: Kemira, the Helsinki based maker of coagulants, flocculants and other chemicals for water intensive industries, employs about 4,900 people. On October 23 it reported third quarter revenue of €709 million, up 3%, with flat organic growth and about €18 million added by acquisitions. Chief executive Antti Salminen kept full year guidance of €2.6 to €3.0 billion in revenue and €400 to €500 million in operative EBITDA.

Water Solutions, its largest segment, grew revenue 5% to €331 million, mainly through acquisitions, with a 19.7% operative EBITDA margin. Kemira closed the purchase of Nebraska based Water Engineering, an industrial water treatment services firm serving food and beverage, manufacturing and healthcare, in October 2025, then added ANMAC Water Treatment Service and Italy's REPUR, which provides activated carbon services, in the third quarter.

The pressure is on costs. Group operative EBITDA margin fell to 15.9% from 20.0% as variable costs rose €35 million against €11 million of price increases, and Kemira puts the gross 2026 cost impact of the Middle East conflict at about €100 million, roughly half of it mitigated. On November 23 it said it will invest in a venture fund to back startup innovation.
supplier.why: Activated carbon and service contracts put Kemira closer to the PFAS and industrial reuse spending wave. Watch whether price increases catch up with input costs in 2027.

innovation.name: University of Rochester
innovation.headline: A Rochester lab desalinates seawater without leaving brine behind
innovation.body: Most desalination plants send concentrated brine back to the sea. A team led by Chunlei Guo at the University of Rochester's Institute of Optics built a solar thermal system that uses no chemical additives and discharges no liquid brine, extracting nearly 100% of the dissolved salts in solid form. It tested real seawater from the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Oceans and published the work in Light: Science & Applications. A related study recovered about half the lithium in salts left after desalination, using Great Salt Lake samples. The work is at laboratory stage, and the release gives no flow rate or cost figures.

investor.name: Burnt Island Ventures
investor.headline: The most active water-only venture firm
investor.body: Founded in New York by water industry veteran Tom Ferguson, Burnt Island invests only in early stage water technology. Xylem anchored both of its funds, with climate fund of funds WovenEarth Ventures joining Fund II. Published deal trackers show 2026 investments in Aquatic Labs, Crew Carbon, Biota and Verdi.

capital.intro: Private equity has executed 435 water deals across 25 countries since 2015 and more than doubled its holdings since 2019, according to Bluefield Research. Most of those assets are under three years old, which points to an exit wave.

firm.headline: XPV is buying the unglamorous middle of the water economy

figs.l: Raised for Fund III and Extended Value Fund

firm.body: XPV invests only in water and builds platforms through add-on acquisitions. In 2026 it bought Weisinger, a groundwater and well services provider for Texas municipal and industrial clients, formed the ocean technology platform OceanSight, and added Sound Metrics and C&C Ground Water Services. In June it exited Axius Water alongside co-owner KKR. Founding partner David Henderson leads the firm.

demand.title: Demand keeps climbing as the world adds two billion people
demand.intro: Global water demand has more than doubled since 1960 and has grown by just under 1% a year since the 1980s. The UN expects the population to rise from 8.2 billion in 2024 to a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid 2080s.

security.headline: The UN says the world has entered water bankruptcy
security.text: A UN University report in January argued that groundwater depletion, overallocation and pollution have pushed many basins past the point of recovery, and that "crisis" no longer describes it.

security.text: The two countries signed a formal agreement in September on new operating guidelines for the river that supplies seven US states and northern Mexico.

security.headline: The Gulf runs on desalination
security.text: The Middle East and North Africa host over 40% of global desalination capacity, and the Gulf Cooperation Council countries alone hold 33%.

place.name: Basilica Cistern
place.headline: A sixth century reservoir held up by a forest of 336 columns
body: Built between 532 and 542 under the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian I, the Basilica Cistern, Yerebatan Sarnıcı in Turkish, was one of the city's major water stores, with an estimated capacity of about 100,000 tons. Its roof rests on 336 columns, each 9 meters tall.

Two carved Medusa heads, identified in 1986, serve as column bases, one upside down and one on its side. The cistern opened to visitors in 1987 after a major restoration, and reopened on July 22, 2022 after a second restoration that began in 2014.
place.visit: In Istanbul's historic peninsula; open as a museum. Check opening hours and tickets before you go.
place.why: Istanbul hosts the IWRA World Water Congress in October 2027, and this is the city's oldest lesson in storing water close to demand.
